name: Bell peppers
tile_uses: Rice bowls, tacos, house flavor, chicken
why_now: Red and yellow bell peppers are fully ripened green peppers — and August is when they arrive in abundance. The color change takes weeks on the plant, which is why they cost more and why they taste completely different. The bitterness is gone. What's left is sweet, thick, and worth roasting.
how_to_choose: Fully red or fully yellow — no green patches
Firm and heavy for their size
The thicker the walls, the better for roasting
buy_this_much: 3–4 peppers for the week. Two go into the house flavor; the rest go into meals.
price_note: Red and yellow peppers cost more than green because they've spent longer on the plant. In August, supply increases and prices tend to soften slightly.

flavor_paths.name: Charred
flavor_paths.description: The house flavor. Blistered in a dry pan, steamed, peeled, blended with garlic, oil, and sherry vinegar.

flavor_paths.name: Raw
flavor_paths.description: Sliced thin in a taco or rice bowl. The sweetness holds without cooking.

flavor_paths.name: Roasted whole
flavor_paths.description: In the oven at high heat. Collapse into softness, serve alongside chicken or fold into pasta.

weekday_uses: Sliced raw into tacos or rice bowls
Roasted and added to a rice bowl or pasta
Used as the base for the charred pepper sauce
weekend_use: Roasted whole alongside chicken thighs. Tear them open over the plate.
storage: Refrigerator crisper. Up to a week before roasting; a few days once roasted.
one_thing_to_learn: A fully red bell pepper and a green bell pepper are the same vegetable at different points of ripeness. The green one was picked early. Weeks more on the plant produce the color, the sweetness, and the complete absence of that grassy bitterness. This is also why charring works so well on red peppers — there's actual sugar to caramelize.
market_question: Are these fully ripened on the plant, or ripened in transit?
